html:
The Lyceum was a gymnasium and grove sacred to Apollo just outside Athens, where Aristotle founded his school in 334 BCE.

Aristotle had studied for twenty years at the Academy of Plato and then tutored the young Alexander. Back in Athens, he taught at the Lyceum while walking up and down its covered walk, the peripatos, so his followers were called the Peripatetics. The school was a place of research as well as teaching. It gathered a large library and collected facts on a huge scale: descriptions of animals, histories, and studies of 158 Greek constitutions, of which the Constitution of the Athenians survives.

When Alexander died in 323 BCE, Aristotle left Athens, and his student Theophrastus led the school, writing the first great works on plants. The school went on for more than two centuries, until the Roman general Sulla destroyed it when he besieged Athens in 86 BCE. Its remains were found in 1996 during building work in the centre of modern Athens.
sum: The Lyceum was a gymnasium and grove sacred to Apollo just outside Athens, where Aristotle founded his school in 334 BCE.
